I was talking about the level of replenishment of the corps forces and the command units at the time I assumed my duties at the corps, and this was the 20th of January. So this is a major time difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now move to 6D1313. This is a Pristina Corps command report -- combat report, pardon me, that at page 2 under the sixth paragraph reports that the -- that in the course of an action in the Runjevo and Stagovo villages, the 243rd Motorised Brigade liquidated five terrorists. Would you agree with me that this Pristina Corps report had to be based on a report from the commander of the 243rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. How else could it be drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the fourth paragraph of section 2.1, can we conclude from what is reported here that in the course of a legitimate -- of a legitimate anti-terrorist action, the 243rd entered both named villages to rout the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way or understand it that way. Terrorists need not necessarily be in the village. Most often they were on the outskirts of the village at elevations, at such places which made it possible for them to fire at members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon this -- strike that. Had, in fact, the commander of the 243rd Brigade not been able to reach his stated objective and had that commander only reached the points of Stara Kacanik and Kamena Glava, would that -- would you expect that and indeed wouldn't that be mandated to be in the combat report?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the commander had to report on the actual situation and what he did as part of the action. I couldn't understand it any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that this combat report relating to this action does not, in fact, reflect any mention of the 243rd Brigade not being able to reach the stated objective and, rather, stopping at Stara Kacanik and Kamena Glava --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. We can all read what it says in the combat report, and this witness now is being asked to speculate. First of all, he should have been asked if he knew about the action and specific details of it in order to be able to put more questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, had such a report from the commander of the 243rd Brigade been received by the Pristina Corps, it would be reflected in combat reports of the Pristina Corps; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can move to my last topic. You testified in direct about Exhibit 5D476, about an order supposedly sent from the MUP staff with which the secretariats of internal affairs, or SUPs, were ordered to plan anti-terrorist actions with specific VJ -- with specific Pristina Corps elements. Do you, sir, or did you have any occasion to physically see with your own eyes any order from the MUP staff for such a thing to take place?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally didn't see such an order, but information came -- the information came from MUP in any case. Thousands and thousands of orders and plans were drafted, so you cannot expect one man to do all of that. This has been -- this is something that was done consistently. It's not just one -- a one-off thing. A plan is what should be expected in the coming period, what to be prepared for in order to be able to plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this list of actions that is here for the various entities --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Wait for my question and then I'll get through with you very quickly. I apologise. Would you agree with me, in fact, looking at this list of actions on this document - and if you need to turn to the other pages, by all means do so - but that a majority of these anti-terrorist actions were, in fact, carried out pursuant to written orders from the Pristina Corps whether the title of the document said "Joint Command" or simply "Pristina Corps"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The planned actions were both for the army and for the MUP, but the plan was such that the police and the military each knew their own plans. But let me be clear. The army did not plan for others other than its own units and commands. This is just a plan, activity, directed at future actions where the military, the army, and the police would both be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, without -- without the need to confront the witness with every document, for the record, we have P1970, relating to action in section 1.1; P1973 for the action at 1.3 in this document; P1878 for the action at 2.2 in this document; P2003 for the action at 2.3 in this document; P1974 for the action at 3.1 in this document; P1975 for the action at 3.4 of the document; and indeed 6D1307 for 3.3 of this document. And with that, I conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Stefanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of VJ actions and operations, many of which you have spoken about, you would sometimes receive post-action or post-operation analyses from the brigade commanders who commanded the action; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the action was completed or is completed, the commanders would submit regular combat reports containing the assessment of the executed action. When they were asked for a separate analysis, they would send analysis of the actions that were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And once a situation of them being asked for separate analysis I would like to show to you. Could we have a look at 2591, that's P2591. Did some commanders in submitting their analysis complain that in many of these actions and operations the VJ was acting in a heavy-handed way and that is using excessive force?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you mean to say "VJ"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The units of the Pristina Corps to be more precise. Before we get to the document, can you just focus on the question I asked you and answer it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, to repeat this because you are asking me about two topics: Analysis and excessive use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As operations officer or chief of the operations section of the corps, did you receive reports or analyses from brigade commanders that many of the operations as planned were conducted by the units of the Pristina Corps using excessive force?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a whole, no, but I have a document in front of me of the 37th Motorised Brigade command where the use of excessive force is being treated in a relative way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you're being asked for your personal recollection and not to refer to the document. It shouldn't have been put on the screen until you had answered the general question, and the general question, you can deal with without reference to this. So did you receive reports that many of the operations or actions I think it means as planned were conducted by units of the Pristina Corps using excessive force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade commanders sent reports to the corps command, and as far as I know, no one reported on using excessive force or too large a force in actions against the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at the document now, and if we could look at page 2 of the English, paragraphs 2 and 4 from the top, and this is at the bottom of the first page of the B/C/S. The third paragraph or dashed paragraph in B/C/S and the fifth dashed paragraph in -- this, without us going -- flipping around the document, is a report for the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade, Colonel Dikovic, and he says: "In our view, the number of units and troops engaged in Kosmac and Cicavica operations, measured against the results achieved, was inappropriate. In other words, 'operations spread across a large area, but the effects of actions aimed at destroying the STS forces were relatively limited.'" ? Is that what you see in your document? Do you see what I just read in the document? And you will see in the --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is just one report from the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade who says here that the use of relatively large forces is here, that is his own opinion. He suggests smaller actions. We're talking about actions here, not operations. Operations are such activities at the operative level, carried out by corps, but brigades would carry out actions, fights and battles. So this is a report that is separate in that sense and he's suggesting a way to be more effective, but it's not something that can be generalised and applied to all units of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you read that paragraph first, paragraph about engaging relatively large forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can read that for ourselves, can we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you want to highlight expressions used in it, that's a matter for you, but we don't need the whole thing read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In most of the operations or in many of the operations and actions that the VJ forces were involved in where they sealed off areas, so to speak, are you aware that these actions or in the course of these actions significant members of the Kosovar Albanian population were expelled from their homes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the areas of combat actions, the population was aware of that and they left the area. So this was not done because of the military, it was done much earlier. When they come and occupy a certain facility in a special area, the Siptar terrorist forces move out or leave the population there, using them as human shields. I said yesterday that whenever the army observed that civilian population was there, they would stop, and this happened in the majority of the cases. I cannot speak about individual instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having seen now the reference in this particular report from a brigade commander about using relatively large forces to fight small terrorist groups, using an elephant to kill a fly, and conducting large-scale mopping-up operations through the area, can you recall now if you got that, this particular analysis?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm seeing this analysis for the first time in its written form. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive any such complaint or opinion orally from any of the brigade commanders or senior members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commanders reported back to the corps commander. They reported back to the corps commander if they observed something particular. At the corps command level we discussed all these important topics and issues that cropped up in the course of the implementation of an assignment. No one said to me that I used large force to destroy a terrorist group, quite to the contrary. There were more commanders who said that they didn't have a sufficient number of forces or a sufficient force size.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Your answer is: No, you weren't aware of these reports. I take it then that you didn't factor into your preparations and your plans the recommendations made by Colonel Dikovic in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him or know anything about his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have seen a series of documents- and I'm moving on to something else now - where the reference number is -- includes the number 455. Perhaps we could look at one, P2808, because I think that one is 455-1. And this is an order I think you said you yourself prepared. I don't think I need to take you back to it. You recall that, don't you? Don't nod. Do not nod. Can you answer verbally?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. How -- what's the significance of the number existing, 455, we have seen many of the orders, how is that decided upon? Is it -- or you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each command organ had its own list of documents and numbers because the operations organ is a large organ and plans a large number of documents and drafts a large number of documents. This is one of those numbers, 455; it's a three-digit number. And this document was registered at this -- with this number. There were also other groups of numbers to record documents in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So do you just give it the number arbitrarily or does the number relate to a topic or is the number -- or it just gets a number sequentially?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is assigned. It's not just made up, it's assigned on the basis of the book of records and then it's allocated to commands, organs, everyone has their own lists of documents and they have their own numbers or several numbers that they use when generating their documents. This number that was used here, I cannot tell you right now why it was 455, but that was the number used for this particular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. And when you see 455-1 here, this would be the first document bearing the 455 number?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, without going into all of these documents, there are documents from March and April bearing 455- various numbers. Does it mean that all of the documents relate back to the original 455 document or are they -- is there a relationship there somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't, because the numbers were also mixed. It would happen because of difficult work conditions and the fact that different people processed the documents. Sometimes the numbers got mixed up, their register numbers. There should have been a number for specific topics, but there were cases when they overlapped or were mixed up with other numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So if, for example, we see 455 with the -- with a report dealing with a laundry list of a unit, that would be a mistake. 455 referred to the specific topic that this order in front of you deals with; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to say, honourable Prosecutor, is that this is a group of numbers that ensures documents to be based on certain numbers and certain groups of numbers. However, as I say, in practice personnel changes, command posts change, there were certain changes and deviations. However, this is the number of the corps command. It cannot be the number of another unit in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. But the question I asked it can be -- I'll ask it this way. Although there might be mistakes in using the number, 455 really should or the intention was that it should refer to the topic that is the subject of the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Many of the documents bearing this number, perhaps all of them, use the expression "armed non-Siptar population," and I think it was your testimony that all documents referring -- or orders arising out of the anti-terrorist combat plan in P2808 had to in the section entered under tasks include reference to the armed non-Siptar population even though you had no authority to command them? That's a correct understanding of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in item 2 of every order of the corps command, or rather, the corps commander, that is the task of the Pristina Corps that was taken over completely from the order of the command of the -- from the commander of the 3rd Army. And this kind of task is taken over in its entirety. The corps commander does not have the right to rephrase that particular item at all, not a single word. Also, if we look at paragraph 4 of the order of the corps commander where the decision is and 5 where the assignments of the units are, there is no reference to the armed population, or rather, the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is what I'm concerned about because your evidence is that you would keep the phrase in although it was meaningless, you couldn't apply it because you had no discretion to take it out. But weren't there Joint Command orders for anti-terrorist actions in which that phrase was not included?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that that is a phrase that was taken over, and I told you why, because one does not have the right to change it. In all orders where there is the task --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. I think there might be a mistranslation. Weren't there Joint Command orders for anti-terrorist operations where the persons who drafted the order exercised their discretion to take it out, didn't include it, include that expression?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No translation on the Serbian channel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try again, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring to your evidence where you said that there was no discretion. All orders under this head had to include in the task section reference to armed non-Siptar population, and I'm saying to you or I'm asking if you were aware that there were orders by the Joint Command for anti-terrorist operations that did not have in the task section this phrase "engage the armed non-Siptar population"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. That phrase pertained only to the task given to the Pristina Corps. It did not pertain to the tasks of units of the brigade and so on. It only pertained to the task of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, but you're not answering my question. My question -- or let's just look at one document, let's look at P3049. You see item 2 on --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a Joint Command order of the 19th of March and it's numbered 455-44. Here there is no order to engage the non-Siptar population, is there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in item 2. Perhaps we could have a look at item 3 and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be quicker if you look at it in the hard copy. Since you have the hard copy in your hands, can you remind us who prepared that order, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was written in the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- were you involved in its preparation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not recall. I think that I personally did not participate in the drafting of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see in section 3 it doesn't include reference to the expression "engage armed non-Siptar population."

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This clause is not in this order, but this order omitted item 3. It's not decision, it is neighbours. So it's not my document because I know the way in which I write documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you notice that this is an order, perhaps you will agree with me, for mainly a simple exercise of unblocking a road, and it was expected that the duration would last one to two days. You will agree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What task do you have in mind here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The primary task was to unblock a road, and it is envisioned that this would take one to two days?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the tasks was to ensure that the roads were accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I suggest to you that the reason in this order or the reason why this order does not make a reference to the use of the armed non-Siptar population is because the armed non-Siptar population were not needed for the realization of this task?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. The armed non-Siptar population was not involved at all under the command of the Pristina Corps. I spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was probably meant was the forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you complete that answer, what was probably meant was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can complete that. The armed non-Siptar population as a phrase, as a category that is provided in the task, as far as the Pristina Corps is concerned -- rather, the Pristina Corps never involved the population, never, not in a single task. Why? What is meant here is the forces of the Federal Ministry of Defence, the civil protection and civil defence. In order to have any command engage them for their own needs, the same forces would have to be resubordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the -- withdrawn. Let's get straight to the document. Could we look at 5D1284. Just for the record, this is an order of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not receive notice regarding this document, but I see that I used it; however, Mr. Stamp did not say that he would be using it but I see now that I did use it in direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I think our notice says as a caveat that we'll probably use anything that is used in chief and then list the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You'll see at item 2 - and if we could go to page 2 in the English, top of page 2 - there is a slightly different formulation. Now, this is something that you were asked quite precisely yesterday by your own counsel. It says here in the English: "In coordinated action the 175th Infantry Brigade, the 549th Motorised Brigade, and armed non-Siptar population, through decisive defence of the state border, prevent raids of NATO forces along the following axes ..." That's a slightly different formulation. Does that indicate to you that the brigade commander was authorising his battalion commanders or subordinate commands to involve or engage the armed non-Siptar population in the coordinated action?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a free formal sentence that the commander, or rather, his command, the commander of the 243rd Brigade entered in this task here; however, without the command of the Pristina Corps' task being involved. They could not introduce what had not been given to them in the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With regard in the same document, page 12 of the English, this is item 8.4 dealing with the anti-nuclear, chemical, and biological support, and that's at page 9 of the B/C/S, you see in the second paragraph in English and the last paragraph of 8.4 it says: "Coordinate action with CZ organs and units in the brigade zone of responsibility in order to help each other ..." Doesn't it here specifically refer to the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and it pertains precisely -- if you allow me. As I said a few moments ago, the armed non-Siptar population, or precisely, the forces of the Ministry of Defence, the civil protection, civil defence and here it says coordination. That is to say that these forces are not subordinated to the brigade, but it is a question of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What are the initials for the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: CZ -- oh, CO, sorry, "civilna odbrana"; "civilna zastita," CZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see here in this order when it refers to civil protection, it refers to them specifically, it doesn't call them armed non-Siptar population. Do you know of a reason why these orders instead of using the term "armed non-Siptar population" do not say: "Engage the civil protection and the civil defence"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a brigade document, a document of the 243rd Brigade. That is how he defined it. He specifically refers to civil protection here because it has to do with protection from chemical agents and so on. So this is a specialised battalion of the ABH. This is just coordination. From here one cannot see that the civil protection is subordinated to the 243rd Motorised Brigade. It only coordinates in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that. I just want you to tell us if you know of any reason why, as this commander has written here, when reference is being made to civil protection and civil defence, these orders don't simply say: Coordinate action or engage the CZ and the CO, instead of employing that phrase "armed non-Siptar population." Do you know of any reason why they just don't use those two initials, CZ and CO?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could not use either one. We show through orders, tasks, and decisions that we are not using either name. We can have a look at many documents, the tasks of the units of the corps, it doesn't say the armed non-Siptar population, it doesn't say civil defence, it doesn't say civil protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. Just focus on my questions. I just showed you this here to show that VJ personnel can refer to an entity or a unit by its proper name. In this order they use "armed non-Siptar population" to refer to one thing, and in this order they're also using the expression CZ for civilian protection. Simply: Do you know of a reason why it is that in the Pristina Corps orders if the expression "armed non-Siptar population" refers to civil protection and civil defence, why they do not use those terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I will try to be as specific as possible. The brigade commander, or rather, his organs took this over without approval from the corps command. He defined this himself without approval. The order of the corps commander. In the decision in the tasks of the units there is not a single formulation, it doesn't say armed non-Siptar population or civil defence or civil protection, except that it appears in paragraph 2 where the task of the corps is and nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Forget about this order. Don't look at it anymore. This is the last time I'm going to ask you this question. Why in those Pristina Corps orders don't they use the expression "engage the CZ and the CO"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely, these are forces of the Ministry of Defence and they are not involved in the Pristina Corps and that is why they were not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you are saying that the armed non-Siptar population are forces of the Ministry of Defence and were not involved in the Pristina Corps; that reason applies both to the expression armed non-Siptar population as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We did not use either formulation, and what is meant are the same forces and these are forces of the Ministry of Defence and this was not used in any situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, there may be some difficulty caused by translation, it's not clear to me, but in the document, as you see before you, the brigade commander has referred to civil protection organs specifically by name. And what Mr. Stamp is asking you is why he should do that rather than refer to armed non-Siptar population. Now, can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, the brigade commander does not have the right to use either formulation. What was not given to him within the task given by the corps commander. It is correct that it says "civil protection" here and it is correct that it says "armed non-Siptar population," but this is what he did on his own bat without the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the brigade commander did not have authority to use either formulation. Are you saying he did not have authority to use the formulation "civil protection"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has the right to use everything in terms of expressions, one and the other and the third one; but when speaking of a concrete task he cannot arbitrarily incorporate anything that was not given to him by his superior commander within the task. And here we can see that it is a question of arbitrariness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different matter. We understand that. The question here is why use two separate expressions for one body, and indeed why use a vague, offensive expression like armed -- or discriminatory expression like "armed non-Siptar population" when you can actually use the proper description "civil protection."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, this formulation at the level of the general -- well, it's the way it is. No one understands it differently. It can only be the forces of the civil protection and the civil defence, in no other way. Formally that is the way it is put at the level of the general, the universal. And then the corps command took this over. They did not incorporate this themselves, they took this over because this stems from the general task that cannot be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could move on, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes -- well, it would be a convenient time to break, if it is for you also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to break again, Mr. Stefanovic, for half an hour. Could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said yesterday that when you took over your role or while you were going through the period of being introduced to your tasks as operations sector chief, you discovered that the peacetime establishment of the VJ or the Pristina Corps was just at about 80 per cent, they had insufficient personnel to realize all their tasks, in particular fighting terrorists. What was the situation on or about the 24th of March in respect to the personnel of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The manning level of the commanding units of the Pristina Corps in late March, which is the period that you referred to, was better. As far as I remember, a new party of soldiers was received from the training centres by way of bringing up manpower levels. Some of the units pursuant to an order of the command, that is, the General Staff, was sent in to reinforce the Pristina Corps. The combat capacity of the corps and the manning levels were definitely raised in relation to what the situation had been in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but in January -- in January, February you said there was 18 per cent -- 80 per cent of its peacetime establishment. By the 24th of March it would be a different situation, wouldn't it? It would be the wartime manning strength. What was the percentage at the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain that it was roughly the same as the peacetime establishment or under the peacetime establishment it would have been 95 to 100 per cent, but I can't be certain without reliable information that I could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say it would be the same, you mean at the 24th of March it would be about 80 per cent of the wartime requirements or wartime establishment?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I'm talking about peacetime establishment for manning levels. The order had not yet been issued, or rather, this is the 24th of March, so some of the units, or rather, the mobilisation was in progress and manning levels were being brought up because on the 24th the air-strikes began and a state of war had been declared. Both the state and the army were switching to wartime organization mode, therefore the manning levels in the corps were being brought up and there was a mobilisation in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many soldiers or how many personnel did the Pristina Corps have under its command on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific about the 24th of March, but it was certainly over 100 per cent; it was 110, 115 per cent, so 10 to 15 per cent over and above what it would have been under the peacetime establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after mobilisation, how many did it have by, say, the end of April?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of April, after the mobilisation round had been completed, certain command units, because not all the units in the entire Pristina Corps had been mobilised at the same time, it was a gradual process unit by unit, command by command, and by the end of April the corps had about 18.000 or 20.000 men, including those reinforcements that had in the meantime arrived in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 18.000 men after mobilisation, is that your evidence? Did I hear that correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain, again, I am not positive. I really can't say without reliable information being available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General Samardzic, the former 3rd Army corps commander, said that the VJ had armed some 47.000 civilians by February 1999. Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of the fact -- I wasn't aware of what General Samardzic said, but I can assume how he arrived at that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did he arrive at that figure?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to break this down. Firstly, the reserve forces of the Pristina Corps number about 11.000 military conscripts. If I still remember correctly, about 9.000 military conscripts were actually mobilised and joined the war units of the Pristina Corps. Next, between 9.000 and 10.000 for the Pristina Military District, their own military conscripts and they mobilised their own units. As in Pristina, there was the defence administration, which was an outpost of the defence ministry, they mobilised between 15.000 and 20.000 men. So we take all of that and we also bear in mind the fact that the police had their own military conscripts on wartime assignments and reserve police squads had been set up, so the rough figure that we arrive at would be roughly the same as that mentioned by General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think I better show you what General Samardzic said because it is apparent from what he said that he was not referring to those groups that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at the record of the session of the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the 2nd of February, 1999, that is the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and that's P931.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think P931 is not on the exhibit list that we got -- oh, right, it was delivered after the witness had been sworn in. It wasn't on the original list, but it was added later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, could we go to page 23 of the English, which is similar to page 21 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Ojdanic says: "I've heard that there are 50.000 armed Serbs." General Samardzic: "Judging by the amount of weapons issued, for now, it's 47.000 ..." "What are the war assignments of these armed Serbs and what is the plan for including them in the units?" General Samardzic: "It was my order and we organized the whole thing, for the defence of Serbian villages, commanders at all levels have been sent out, they're armed and they have two combat sets of ammunition each. Their role and assignment is to defend their villages and participate together with army units in operations in the immediate vicinity." For emphasis I repeat: "And participant together with army units in any operations in the immediate vicinity. We have to carry out military and police operations, it can't be done in any other way, and at this moment there are not -- and at this moment there are enough army and MUP members to do their part of the job ..." Do you find that there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that, but I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm just showing that to you. Can you just read for me the last sentence of what General Samardzic says where he says: "We have to carry out military and police operations ..." Can you read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We have to carry out military and police operations, it can't be done in any other way, and at this moment there are enough army and MUP members to do their part of the job if it should come to that."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you will agree with me that those entities that you referred to, the military department, the military police - may I just get the record - the military conscripts, the military -- the personnel of the Pristina Military District, defence administration, they are not engaged in arming Serbs to protect villages; they recruit citizens. As a matter of fact, the evidence is that they tried to recruit non-Serbs, they tried to recruit Albanians. So you will agree with me that General Samardzic, when he speaks of 47.000, is not referring to those groups that you just mentioned. Do you have any idea who General Samardzic was referring to when he said that they have armed 47.000 Serbs for the defence of Serbian villages and to participate with the army units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that this was the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with what I just suggested?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on. You said in respect to P1967, which is an amendment to a previous order, I remember you discussed that, that -- and perhaps we could bring it up, P1967. In regard to this action you said that the command post was at Lausa.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. I said that the command post of the 354th Brigade was at Lausa, and the group of officers designated by the corps commander to go to that command post was to lead the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we have the wrong document here. P1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that command post where the group of officers designated by the corps command went to and where they were joined, I think you said, by officers of the MUP, that is not apparent from this order or this amendment, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't say here that the group was set up and dispatched, but there was an oral order by the corps commander, the group was set up and it was dispatched to the command post in the Lausa sector, or to be even more specific, the Lausko Brdo sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So basically as far as the reference to Lausa in this order is concerned, there is no amendment in respect to that command post because it's not referred to here?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could, therefore, move on more generally to the issue of the Joint Command. When was the first time you heard that expression in relation to Pristina Corps activities with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was when I was taking over my duties from General Djakovic. When I was looking at documents I noticed this header saying "the Joint Command"; and then he told me that this was coordination between the army and the MUP in carrying out anti-terrorist combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were introduced to this term in January, I take it, of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the take-over, hand-over of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many orders emanating from the Pristina Corps headed "Joint Command" did you see in January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several, as far as I can remember, but I can't be more specific than that, several.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We have tried, I can tell you, we have tried to get as many of them as we can and -- well, let me ask you this: You saw several. Can you recall approximately when the earliest was dated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can. It was probably back in 1998, but I really can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was your predecessor, Djakovic, a colonel at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when I was taking over, and this was January 1999, he was already a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long had he held that post at the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think over a year, but I'm not certain. It was over a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you know where he had been before that, immediately before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know where he had been before he came to the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it that you would have been informed that these Pristina Corps documents that were headed "Joint Command" that were issued in 1998 would have been issued by General Pavkovic, who in 1998 was the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Pavkovic was the corps commander in 1998. When I had a chance to go through the documents, I saw that they were from 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you saw these documents saying that they are from the -- or being issued by the Joint Command and they -- and saying at the end that the Joint Command shall command the forces, did you inquire what this Joint Command was all about?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked General Djakovic what this meant - it wasn't common at all - and he said that this was no more than a reference to situations where army units and military [as interpreted] units act together in order to carry out anti-terrorist actions, and he said the name was used only in relation to those situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, did he say army units and military units, in line 73, 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that what you meant, army units and military units or did you mean army units and MUP units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about the army and the police, their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that you thought it to be an unfortunate term; is that what you thought at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I'm not sure I thought that at the time, but I certainly do now. This is something that is irregular as a name, it's something that was simply made up and was ill-founded because it expressed nothing of the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you nonetheless continued to use the computer template, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I would add something there. General Djakovic and the operatives from the army command were there all the time and we planned those actions together. There was a continuity to our work, until such time as the order was issued on resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did General Djakovic, in briefing you about this term "Joint Command," during the hand-over or in those many contacts you had with him which you just indicated now, tell you that the Joint Command included politicians?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was never discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he, in showing you documents from 1998, show you minutes of meetings with the commander of the PrK, General Pavkovic; with General Lukic; Mr. Sainovic; Mr. Minic; Mr. Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Language again, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Fila resents your referring to these as "minutes."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient if we refer to them as notes of the meeting. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- capable of further interpretation in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he show you notes of meetings involving the command of the Pristina Corps; the MUP staff for Kosovo, Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up P1468, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While that's happening, can I clarify one thing with you. You said that "General Djakovic and the operatives from the army command were there all the time and we planned these actions together." Now, in that context are you referring to him and others from the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, precisely. General Djakovic, together with a group of operatives at the command post of the Pristina Corps directly took part in the planning of operations with the operatives of the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From February onwards, all the time, up until the 10th of June, or rather, 15th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back just slightly also, Mr. Stefanovic, there -- you referred to the resubordination order, and that date I assume to be the 20th of April. Were there Joint Command documents after the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, after the 20th of April, or rather, after the resubordination order was issued concerning the MUP, as far as I know, there were no other combat documents of this kind that were drafted and issued with that kind of heading and wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness says that Djakovic did not talk to him about any kind of notes, I don't understand why this is being shown to him now, on the basis of what. It's on the screen. A bit of caution or could the Prosecutor at least explain to us why he is showing this and what is the foundation for that. You already have the answer, that Djakovic never talked to him about any kind of notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not necessarily the end of the inquiry in regard to these notes or their contents with a view to establishing facts, and there can be no objection in general to the use of this exhibit. If a particular question is asked that raises issues of relevance, then you can renew your objection. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we look at page 2 of that -- of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now that you see the document, does that refresh your memory? Do you know this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure whose handwriting this is. We drafted our documents on computers. I didn't have occasion to see people's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And having seen this, you are saying you are not familiar with it? Colonel Djakovic didn't show this to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not have an occasion to see this document because it was not an official document that was handed over during hand-over, if there was something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, whether you saw the document or not, your hand-over lasted one month, you said. Were you told about these meetings at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we didn't have time to talk about that. There were so many tasks that we worked, each one of us, on his own. We could barely have a cup of coffee together during the course of the day. There were so many things that had to be done. I had so many things to do, and there was a pile of documents to look at in addition to the work I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have had evidence here of a meeting on the 1st of June, 1999, in Pristina at the Grand Hotel, where the leaders of the Pristina Corps as well as the 3rd Army and the commanders of the MUP and Mr. Sainovic attended, and Mr. Sainovic is supposed to have spoken at that meeting. Did you hear about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, honourable Prosecutor. On the 1st of June, the date that you referred to, I was leading the Drenica 1 action so I was not at the corps command at all on that day, or rather, during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you return to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think sometime around the 5th or the 6th of June, after a few days, a few days after that action, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you attend any collegium meetings of the Pristina Corps in early June 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war special collegium meetings were not held. It was meetings in the morning and in the evening depending on the extent to which the commander could bring all the organs of the command together, in view of the fact that most of the organs of the command were in the subordinate units. However, there weren't any collegium meetings in the classical sense, like in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There weren't weekly collegium meetings that you attended at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, no, there weren't any collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General Lazarevic testified and he indicated that it was his operation sector staff who met with the MUP for coordination, you would be meeting with the MUP to coordinate. Now, in these coordination meetings, did you meet with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, except when I came to the command of the Pristina Corps with General Djakovic, I went to the staff, and that's where I met the man. We said hello, and that was it. Never again did we have an opportunity to see each other during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did your deputy meet with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, which -- at General Lukic's level, General Lukic was the head or the chief of the MUP staff of Kosovo and Metohija. What was the corresponding level in the Pristina Corps or the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have to object to this question since the witness is a -- is not a member of the Ministry of the Interior and I believe he even testified in his direct about the different structures of the army and the police, and so I don't think he's in a position to opine as to whether, in fact, there is a corresponding level between the -- between any position in the MUP and any position in the army for that matter. So I think this question is objectionable on that ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has indicated that himself and other members of the MUP -- of the VJ and the Pristina Corps met with MUP officers for the purposes of coordinating. He therefore should be in a position to opine or state what he understood to be the situation at that time, whether he's right or wrong, but what he understood the situation to be at that time is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow you to ask that question. You're aware of the limitations upon the answer, but perception I think is -- of Mr. Stefanovic is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was at a similar level to Major -- sorry, withdrawn. As you understood it in 1999 during the war, which VJ officer would be of a corresponding level to General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not simple to answer just like that because the structures are terribly different in terms of organization and also in terms of level. So it's impossible to say anything that would be relevant and truthful. This is a separate structure, the police is, and the army is established in a different way when compared to the police. So I cannot establish a counterpart of General Lukic's from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of General Lukic meeting with anybody from the Pristina Corps or from the VJ during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said earlier on, I saw General Lukic only once, that's when we met, we said hello, and as far as I know since I was in charge of my organs no one had occasion to meet with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is something that needs to be clarified here. When you were asked about the coordination at a high level and you gave the answer that you've just given, you actually said when you were asked if you had met Lukic: "No, Mr. Prosecutor, except when I came to the command of the Pristina Corps with General Djakovic. I went to the staff and that's where I met the man. We said hello and that was it." Now, is that what you actually said "when I came to the command of the Pristina Corps"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that when you first arrived in January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, precisely when I came to take over my duties as chief of the organ within the hand-over of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, let's go back to the original question: "General Lazarevic testified and he indicated it was his operations sector staff who met with the MUP for coordination." Now, who was it in your staff that met the MUP -- who was the most senior person in your staff that met the MUP for coordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I was the highest level from my organ a few times, and my deputy, and a few other officers from the operations organ, along with officers from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who -- from the MUP, who was the most senior MUP officer that you met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, it was General Obrad Stevanovic, he was the highest, then Brakovic and then Lieutenant-Colonel Arsenijevic. Those are the three persons who I had a chance to meet and to coordinate a certain number of actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who in your staff met General Lukic for coordination? Was there anyone did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, none of my staff, none of my staff went to this coordination because there wasn't coordination with General Lukic directly, as far as I know, from my level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, can you just deal with this issue and then we'll finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you understand General Lukic's role to be during the intervention in 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was heading the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for Kosovo and Metohija, and I didn't know anything else about the purview of that staff and what their duties were. I did not have occasion to talk or to familiarise myself with it. I was just an operations officer, a colonel, in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As operations officer, yourself and many of the senior persons in the Pristina Corps, you primarily made efforts, according to you, to resolve this resubordination issue with the MUP. Did no one in the Pristina Corps, to your knowledge, meet with General Lukic in respect to this?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that I had most contacts, but as assigned by the corps commander in order to resolve the problem of resubordinating the MUP, but I really do not know whether someone else had contacts of coordination because I really don't know. I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you were the operations officer. It was your responsibility to know what steps were being taken in respect to resubordination, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's what I did. That is mostly what I did, but as assigned by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when, according to you, you were told that no orders had come down to the units in the field for resubordination, you are saying that you don't know if anybody in the Pristina Corps asked Mr. Lukic about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Had this happened in peacetime, I would have certainly known a lot more, but in a war situation bombs and rockets are falling every day, day and night. People are losing their lives every day and the command post is moving several times during the day. We see the commander only for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Arsenijevic, he is -- he was a part of the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps this might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stefanovic, that completes our session for today again, I'm afraid because there's another case this afternoon, we have to interrupt at this stage. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00, again 9.00 in this courtroom tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two -- yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just quickly, we sent an e-mail to everyone due to travel constraints our order of witnesses has changed so that Mr. Paunovic will be our first witness rather than Mr. Joksic. Just wanted to bring that to Your Honour's attention as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have an opening to make or straight into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Straight into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one other -- well, two other matters of concern, one affecting you. Outstanding is the identification of some of your witnesses, the PJP chiefs I think in four areas. Now, as we did before, unless this can be resolved soon, then we will exclude any reference to them from the 65 ter list and once you have identified suitable witnesses you will have to apply to amend the 65 ter list, but you can let me know tomorrow whether that process will be necessary or whether you can do this now. The other matter concerns Mr. Visnjic. We have not yet received the untranslated documents which you seek to have admitted from the bar table, and time is passing and that sort of thing really needs to be resolved finally. Now, can you indicate when we will receive the motion to deal with these?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a matter of days, within a few days, we're expecting two or three translations, but we have already received the longest translation and we wish to disclose it today to the Prosecution. So it will be done within two or three days. There are a few combat reports that are left for translation, but it's going to be a bit of a complex request and it's going to contain most of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have that then in a week?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So next Wednesday dead-line for that. Thank you. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
